title: Cal/OSHA Wildfire Smoke Rule: What Contractors Must Do at AQI 151
dek: At a PM2.5 AQI of 151, California crews must get AQI checks, training and N95s for voluntary use. Above 500, respirators are required.
keyPoints: The rule (Title 8, Section 5141.1) applies when the current AQI for PM2.5 is 151 or higher and you can reasonably expect crews to be exposed.
Check AQI at the start of each shift and periodically after, using AirNow.gov or another approved source.
From AQI 151 to 500, NIOSH-approved respirators such as N95s must be provided for voluntary use and employees encouraged to wear them.
Above AQI 500, respirator use is required.
Crews exposed for one hour or less per shift, or working in filtered buildings or vehicles with closed windows, are exempt.

sources.title: Protecting Outdoor Workers Exposed to Smoke from Wildfires
Employer Requirements Under Cal OSHA's Wildfire Smoke Regulation - Liebert Cassidy Whitmore
Appendix B to Section 5141.1 Protection from Wildfire Smoke

body: California's wildfire smoke regulation, Title 8 Section 5141.1, covers outdoor work whenever the current Air Quality Index for PM2.5 is 151 or greater and an employer can reasonably expect workers to be exposed to wildfire smoke. For roofers, solar installers, HVAC techs on condensers, and anyone framing or trenching outside, that means smoke days carry specific duties, and they start before the first truck rolls.

The rule has a few exemptions. Workers in enclosed buildings where a mechanical ventilation system filters the air and openings are kept closed are not covered. Neither are workers in vehicles with cabin air filtration and closed windows and doors. Employees exposed for one hour or less during a shift are also exempt. Most installation crews spend far more than an hour outside, so plan as if the rule applies.

Step 1: Check the AQI at the start of every shift. Cal/OSHA lets you use AQI forecasts or current readings from EPA's AirNow, the U.S. Forest Service, or state and local air districts, or a direct-reading instrument. Enter the jobsite zip code, since conditions can differ a lot between the shop and a site 30 miles away. Check again during the day as conditions change.

Step 2: Tell the crew. You need a system for letting employees know the current PM2.5 AQI and what protections are available, in a language they understand. Employees must be able to report worsening air or symptoms such as trouble breathing without fear of reprisal.

Step 3: Train before smoke season, not during it. Training follows Appendix B of the regulation and covers the health effects of smoke, how to check the AQI, your communication system, how to get and wear respirators properly, and the right to medical treatment without retaliation.

Step 4: Reduce exposure where you can. Engineering controls come first when feasible, such as moving work into filtered enclosed spaces or vehicles. When those cannot bring exposure under AQI 151, change the work: reschedule outdoor tasks, shorten time outside, move a crew to an indoor job, or provide more breaks in a cleaner location.

Step 5: Provide respirators. From AQI 151 through 500, employers must provide NIOSH-approved filtering facepiece respirators such as N95s for voluntary use and encourage employees to wear them. Approved types include N95, N99, N100, R95, P95, P99 and P100. When the AQI exceeds 500, respirator use becomes required. Keep a box of N95s in every truck through fall so supply is never the reason a crew goes without.

A few practical habits help. Put the AQI check into the morning dispatch routine or the daily job log in your field software so there is a record. Brief foremen on the 151 and 500 thresholds. Plan alternate indoor or service work for smoke days so lost outdoor hours do not become lost payroll.
This is general information from Cal/OSHA materials. For questions about your own crews, contact Cal/OSHA Consultation Services or a safety professional.
Today's next step: bookmark AirNow on every foreman's phone and confirm each truck has a sealed box of N95 respirators.
